name: Histories of Herodotus
info: The Histories is a Greek prose inquiry by Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484 – c. 425 BCE) into the rise of the Persian Empire and the Greco-Persian Wars, regarded as the founding work of history in Western literature.

facts.made: Herodotus of Halicarnassus, who claimed to have travelled widely and gathered accounts by interview, working from an Ionian tradition of story-telling, from Homer and from Athenian tragedy
facts.form: A Greek prose work, Historíai, divided at some point into the nine books of modern editions, conventionally named after the nine Muses
facts.where: The oldest surviving manuscripts are Byzantine copies of the 9th and 10th centuries, among them the Codex Laurentianus A; early papyri include Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 18, 19 and 2099
facts.known: The rise of Persia and the Greco-Persian Wars; the Croesus and Solon story; the account of Egypt and the Nile; the Scythians; Thermopylae, Salamis and Plataea; the tale of Arion and the dolphin; the stories of giant gold-digging ants

t: Herodotus set out to keep human deeds from fading with time and to explain, among other things, why Greeks and non-Greeks went to war with each other.
The work ranges over Lydia, Persia, Egypt, Scythia and the Greek cities, and builds to the invasion of Greece under Xerxes and the Greek victories at Salamis, Plataea and Mycale.
Its reliability has been disputed since antiquity, yet it remains the primary, often only, source for much of the Greek world and the Persian Empire in the two centuries before his time.
dyk: Herodotus reported giant, fox-sized "ants" in an eastern province of the Persian Empire that unearthed gold dust. After journeys in northern Pakistan, Michel Peissel proposed that he may have meant the Himalayan marmot, whose burrows bring gold dust to the surface on the Deosai Plateau.
ev: Nothing in the Histories can be dated with certainty later than this year, and Herodotus is generally assumed to have died not long afterwards
Aristophanes' comedy The Acharnians blames the Peloponnesian War on the abduction of some prostitutes, a mocking reference to the opening of the Histories
Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 2099 preserves a fragment of Book VIII
The oldest extant manuscripts of the Histories, including the Codex Laurentianus A, date from the 9th and 10th centuries, in the Byzantine period
Gelonus, the Scythian city Herodotus described, is rediscovered

sections.origins:
Herodotus of Halicarnassus lived from about 484 to about 425 BCE. He claimed to have travelled extensively around the ancient world, conducting interviews and collecting stories, and almost all of the territory the Histories covers lay within the Persian Empire. The opening lines state his purpose: to prevent the traces of human events from being erased by time, to preserve the fame of the important and remarkable achievements of both Greeks and non-Greeks, and to set out in particular the cause of the hostilities between them.

He had predecessors in prose. Hecataeus of Miletus began his Genealogies with the words "I write these things as they seem true to me; for the stories told by the Greeks are various and in my opinion absurd." Herodotus mentions Hecataeus twice, once mocking his naive genealogy and once quoting Athenian complaints about his handling of their national history, and it is possible that he borrowed much from him. Hecataeus, however, did not record events within living memory, and he did not set Greek oral traditions inside a wider history of the East. There is no proof that Herodotus took the scope of his own work, a grand theme of civilisations in conflict, from any predecessor.

Poets and story-tellers shaped him as well. Athenian tragedy gave him a world-view in which conflicting forces balance until the hubris of kings upsets them, and a model for episodic structure; passages echo Aeschylus's Persae. Homer was another source of inspiration, and Herodotus appears to have drawn on an Ionian tradition of story-telling in the way Homer drew on oral poetry.
sections.content:
The Histories is one of the earliest accounts of the rise of the Persian Empire and of the events and causes of the Greco-Persian Wars of the 5th century BCE. Herodotus portrays the conflict as one between the forces of slavery, the Persians, and the forces of freedom, the Athenians and the confederacy of Greek city-states that united against the invaders. The nine books bear the names of the Muses. Book I (Clio) begins with the abductions of Io, Europa and Medea and moves through the rulers of Lydia, Croesus and the oracle at Delphi to Cyrus II of Persia, the Medes and Babylon. Book II (Euterpe) turns to the geography, customs and kings of Egypt, and Book III (Thalia) to Cambyses, the conspiracy against the Magi, the rise of Darius I and the twenty satrapies.

Book IV (Melpomene) is chiefly about the Scythians and Darius's failed attack on them. Book V (Terpsichore) covers the revolt of Miletus and the burning of Sardis, and Book VI (Erato) the defeat of the Ionian fleet and the Athenian victory at Marathon under Miltiades. Book VII (Polymnia) follows Xerxes' preparations, including his canal and bridges across the Hellespont, and the battle of Thermopylae. In its summary, a Greek force of about 7,000 under Leonidas I faces a Persian army that Herodotus puts at about 5,283,220. Book VIII (Urania) describes the Greek fleet under Eurybiades, the evacuation and destruction of Athens and the battle of Salamis, and Book IX (Calliope) the death of Mardonius at Plataea and the Greek victory at Mycale.

Each book also holds digressions, among them the tale of Arion carried to shore by a dolphin and an account of the Persian royal road from Sardis to Susa.
sections.making:
The Histories was at some point divided into nine books, the form found in modern editions. His preamble sets out his purpose as explanation: he discusses the reason or cause of events. This mode of explanation traces itself back to Homer, who opened the Iliad with a question of causality, as Herodotus does when he asks why Greeks and barbarians went to war. His explanations cover a host of causes and emotions; it has been noted that the obligations of gratitude and revenge are for him fundamental human motives. Some readers hold that his habit of tying events to personal motives shows an inability to see broader reasons, while John Gould argues that he gave the rational reasons as his contemporaries understood them.

He attributes cause to both divine and human agents, not as exclusive alternatives but as interconnected. Geoffrey de Ste-Croix and Mabel Lang have argued that Fate is his ultimate understanding of causality, whereas Gould places him in a long line of story-tellers whose sense of what was "going to happen" belongs to narrative, not to a theory of historical necessity.

Herodotus uses, or claims to use, various sources. At times he sets out several accounts of one story, as with the Phoenician and Persian accounts of Io, and at times he arbitrates between them or claims authority, saying he heard something from the Delphians themselves. He probably knew no language but Greek and relied on translators within the multilingual Persian Empire. His reports on Greek events draw heavily on Periclean Athens and are often coloured by Athenian bias against Thebes and Corinth.
sections.reception:
The accuracy of the Histories has been controversial since his own era. In antiquity Herodotus acquired a reputation as unreliable, biased and mendacious. Duris of Samos called him a "myth-monger", Cicero said his works were full of legends or fables, the grammarian Harpocration wrote a book on "the lies of Herodotus", and Lucian of Samosata denied him a place among the famous on the Island of the Blessed. Aristotle, Flavius Josephus and Plutarch also commented on the dispute. Thucydides was often preferred for truthfulness and reliability, even though he continued on foundations Herodotus had laid. Yet many, among them Strabo, routinely cited Herodotus, and he was in general held in high esteem.

Charges of bias were made too. A work titled On the Malice of Herodotus, attributed to Plutarch or to a pseudonymous author, alleged prejudice against Thebes, and a Corinthian Oration ascribed to Dio Chrysostom, or to another writer, alleged prejudice against Corinth. Plutarch called him philobarbaros, a pro-foreigner.

Some modern scholars still hold parts of the work unreliable. Detlev Fehling argues that Herodotus exaggerated the extent of his travels and invented his sources, and concludes that the work is intended as fiction; Boedeker agrees that much of it consists of literary devices. Alan B. Lloyd calls the work seriously defective as a historical document on Egypt. Others, among them Cheikh Anta Diop and Derek A. Welsby, defend his Egyptian and Nile material as careful and corroborated. Modern historians generally take a more positive view of its value as a source and have called him the father of comparative anthropology and of ethnography.
sections.survival:
The oldest extant copies of the Histories are Byzantine manuscripts of the 9th and 10th centuries, notably the Codex Laurentianus A. Many early papyri also survive, including Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 18 and 19 and Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 2099, a fragment of Book VIII from the early 2nd century CE.

Several of the work's claims have been tested against later finds. Discoveries made since the end of the 19th century have generally added to Herodotus's credibility. He described Gelonus, in Scythia, as a city thousands of times larger than Troy, which was widely disbelieved until it was rediscovered in 1975. The archaeological study of the now-submerged Egyptian city of Heracleion, and the recovery of the so-called Naucratis stela, support his claim that Heracleion was founded during the Egyptian New Kingdom. A baris, a kind of boat the Histories describes, was found during excavation at the sunken port of Thonis-Heracleion.

Other passages remain disputed. Herodotus claimed to have visited Babylon but does not mention the Hanging Gardens, which has fed attacks on his credibility; Dalley has proposed that the Gardens stood at Nineveh instead. His story of gold-digging ants was repeated by Pliny the Elder in the Naturalis Historia, and Michel Peissel suggested that the marmots of the Deosai Plateau lay behind it, perhaps through a confusion of the Persian words for marmot and mountain ant. Herodotus did not claim to have seen the creatures himself.
sections.legacy:
The Histories is considered the founding work of history in Western literature. Although it is not an impartial record, it remains one of the West's most important sources and established the genre and study of history in the Western world. For the Greek world, the Persian Empire and the wider region in the two centuries before his time it has long served, and still serves, as the primary and often the only source. The Greek word historia, meaning research, gave the English word history.

Historians and thinkers have drawn on it in many ways. A. H. L. Heeren quoted it throughout his work, and writers on Egypt and Africa, among them Constantin François de Chassebœuf, comte de Volney, and W. E. B. Du Bois, valued its contribution to the history and ethnography of the Nile valley. Martin Bernal relied on it heavily in Black Athena. Herodotus has been called the "father of history" and described as more modern than any other ancient historian in his approach to the ideal of total history.

Barry S. Strauss writes that Herodotus is one of the great storytellers and a philosopher with three themes: the struggle between East and West, the power of liberty, and the rise and fall of empires. John Herington described him as a centaur, a historian's human forepart joined to a body from an older and wilder realm of tale and myth. Historical novels also take material from the work.

summary: The Histories is Herodotus's Greek inquiry into the rise of the Persian Empire and the causes and course of the Greco-Persian Wars. Its reliability has been disputed since antiquity, yet it remains the primary source for much of its period and is regarded as the founding work of Western history.
